blocks.text: A 45-year-old woman with severe Crohn disease, unresponsive to conventional drugs, is offered an infusion of an antibody against tumour necrosis factor. Before the first dose she has a chest X-ray, a blood test for tuberculosis infection and hepatitis B serology. A single targeted antibody can transform the disease, but it also removes a defence that the body relies on.

blocks.markdown: A **monoclonal antibody (mAb)** is an antibody produced by a single clone of B cells, so every molecule is identical and recognises the same epitope. Unlike polyclonal antisera, mAbs are consistent and can be made in large quantity. They are used therapeutically to neutralise soluble mediators, block receptors, deplete cells or deliver payloads. **Biologics** is the broader term for drugs made from living systems, including mAbs and fusion proteins.

**Production: the hybridoma.** In 1975 Köhler and Milstein showed that a B cell from an immunised mouse could be fused with an immortal myeloma cell to form a **hybridoma**, which makes one antibody indefinitely. Fused cells are separated from unfused cells using selective **HAT medium** (hypoxanthine, aminopterin, thymidine): unfused myeloma cells, lacking the salvage enzyme, die, and unfused B cells die naturally; only hybridomas survive. Individual clones are screened for the desired antibody and grown. Modern production also uses **phage display** and **transgenic mice** carrying human immunoglobulin genes, and the antibody genes are expressed in cultured mammalian cells.

**The problem of immunogenicity.** Mouse antibodies are foreign to humans: the patient may make **anti-drug antibodies** (human anti-mouse antibodies) that neutralise the drug, shorten its half-life and cause hypersensitivity reactions. Engineering therefore replaced mouse sequence with human sequence as far as possible, and the **suffix of the drug name** records how much is human.

Only the mouse CDRs grafted onto a human framework
blocks.caption: Naming of monoclonal antibodies by origin

blocks.title: Read the name
blocks.text: The letters before 'mab' tell you the source: -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab human. A middle infix sometimes indicates the target class (for example -li- for immune system, -tu- for tumour).

blocks.title: Decode the drug
blocks.prompt: Identify the likely origin of (a) infliximab, (b) adalimumab and (c) trastuzumab, and say which is expected to be least immunogenic.

steps.text: (a) infliximab ends in -ximab: a chimeric antibody with mouse variable regions and human constant regions.
(c) trastuzumab ends in -zumab: humanised, only the CDRs are murine.
Rank: the more human sequence, the lower the expected immunogenicity, so the fully human adalimumab is expected to be least immunogenic, though anti-drug antibodies can still develop.

blocks.answer: (a) chimeric, (b) fully human, (c) humanised; (b) is least immunogenic.

blocks.markdown: **Anti-TNF therapy.** Tumour necrosis factor (TNF) is a pro-inflammatory cytokine made mainly by macrophages and T cells. It exists as a membrane-bound and a soluble form, signalling through TNF receptors to activate NF-κB, induce other cytokines (IL-1, IL-6), increase endothelial adhesion molecules and recruit leucocytes. In rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, psoriasis and ankylosing spondylitis, excessive TNF drives chronic inflammation. **Infliximab** (chimeric, intravenous) and **adalimumab** (fully human, subcutaneous) bind soluble and membrane TNF, preventing it from engaging its receptors. **Etanercept** is a different type of biologic: a fusion protein of the TNF receptor and IgG Fc, which acts as a decoy for soluble TNF.

**Why infection screening is needed.** TNF is essential for forming and maintaining the **granulomas** that wall off *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*; anti-TNF therapy therefore risks **reactivation of latent tuberculosis**, often with disseminated or extrapulmonary disease. **Hepatitis B** can also reactivate during immunosuppression. Other serious infections (bacterial, fungal such as histoplasmosis, and viral) occur more often. **Before starting**, guidelines call for screening: TB (history, an interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin test, and chest imaging), hepatitis B (HBsAg and anti-HBc), and commonly hepatitis C and HIV; vaccination status is reviewed, and **live vaccines are avoided** during therapy. Latent TB is treated before or alongside starting a biologic.

Reactivation with immune suppression, risk of liver failure
Live vaccines contraindicated on therapy; inactivated vaccines preferred

blocks.title: Pharmacology teaching example: weight-based dose
blocks.prompt: (Teaching arithmetic only; not dosing advice.) A mAb is dosed at 5 mg/kg for a 70 kg patient. It is supplied as a solution of 10 mg/mL. Calculate the dose and the volume.

steps.text: Dose equals dose per kg times mass.
Volume equals dose divided by concentration.
The calculation illustrates why dose varies with body mass for intravenous antibodies, whereas fixed-dose subcutaneous antibodies need no such calculation.

blocks.title: Other hazards of anti-TNF therapy
blocks.text: Infusion reactions, anti-drug antibodies with loss of effect, new-onset or worsening demyelinating disease, worsening of heart failure at higher doses, and drug-induced lupus-like syndromes have been described. These are reasons for specialist supervision.

points: Monoclonal antibodies derive from a single B cell clone; hybridoma technology fuses an antibody-producing B cell with a myeloma cell and uses HAT selection.
Drug names indicate origin: -omab murine, -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, -umab fully human.
Anti-TNF drugs neutralise TNF in inflammatory disease; screening for tuberculosis and hepatitis B (and HIV/HCV) and avoiding live vaccines are required before treatment.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a hybridoma?

options.text: A fusion of an antibody-producing B cell with an immortal myeloma cell that secretes a single antibody
A fusion of two T cells
A bacterial cell expressing TNF
A plasma cell that makes IgE

questions.correctOptionText: A fusion of an antibody-producing B cell with an immortal myeloma cell that secretes a single antibody

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this gives a cell line making one monoclonal antibody indefinitely.
distractorRationale.b: T cells do not make antibody.
distractorRationale.c: It is not a bacterial cell.
distractorRationale.d: A hybridoma is not defined by IgE.

questions.explanation: Hybridomas result from fusing an antibody-secreting B cell with an immortal myeloma cell, giving a cell line that produces identical antibody.

questions.stem: A drug is named 'xyzumab'. Which description fits?

options.text: Mouse antibody
Chimeric with mouse variable regions
Humanised
Fully human antibody

distractorRationale.d: Correct: -umab denotes a fully human antibody.

questions.explanation: The letters before 'mab' encode origin: -omab murine, -ximab chimeric, -zumab humanised, and -umab human.

questions.stem: Why was a chimeric or humanised design adopted instead of using mouse antibodies?

options.text: To reduce immunogenicity and anti-drug antibodies and prolong half-life
To make the drug bind complement less
To turn the antibody into an IgM
To allow oral administration

questions.correctOptionText: To reduce immunogenicity and anti-drug antibodies and prolong half-life

distractorRationale.a: Correct: more human sequence is less immunogenic, with longer half-life.
distractorRationale.b: Binding complement is not the aim.
distractorRationale.c: Class is unrelated to the naming aim.

questions.explanation: Mouse antibodies provoke human anti-mouse antibodies that neutralise the drug and cause reactions; humanising reduces this problem.

questions.stem: Which best describes the primary mechanism of infliximab in Crohn disease?

options.text: Binding and neutralising TNF, preventing receptor signalling
Blocking the IL-2 receptor
Depleting B cells via CD20
Inhibiting calcineurin

questions.correctOptionText: Binding and neutralising TNF, preventing receptor signalling
questions.explanation: Infliximab binds soluble and membrane TNF, preventing it from signalling through its receptors and thereby reducing inflammation.

questions.stem: Why must latent tuberculosis be sought before starting anti-TNF therapy?

options.text: TNF maintains granulomas, so blocking it can allow latent infection to reactivate
Anti-TNF drugs cause tuberculosis by themselves
TB is the indication for anti-TNF therapy
Anti-TNF drugs are active against tuberculosis

questions.correctOptionText: TNF maintains granulomas, so blocking it can allow latent infection to reactivate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: granuloma integrity depends on TNF.
distractorRationale.b: The drug does not cause infection de novo.
distractorRationale.c: TB is a complication, not an indication.
distractorRationale.d: Anti-TNF drugs have no anti-mycobacterial effect.

questions.explanation: TNF is needed to form and maintain granulomas that contain Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Blocking TNF can allow reactivation and dissemination, so screening is mandatory.

questions.stem: True or false: hepatitis B reactivation is a recognised risk of immunosuppressive biologic therapy, so hepatitis B serology is checked before treatment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Immunosuppression can allow reactivation of latent hepatitis B, sometimes with severe liver injury, so HBsAg and anti-HBc are routinely checked before biologic therapy.

questions.stem: (Teaching arithmetic only.) A monoclonal antibody is dosed at 3 mg/kg for a patient weighing 82 kg. It is supplied at 20 mg/mL. What volume of solution in mL contains the dose?
questions.explanation: Dose = 3 mg/kg × 82 kg = 246 mg. Volume = 246 mg ÷ 20 mg/mL = 12.3 mL. Actual dosing follows product labelling and local protocols.

questions.stem: Describe how monoclonal antibodies are produced by hybridoma technology and explain the naming convention for origin.
markingGuide: Immunise a mouse; fuse spleen B cell with myeloma cell
HAT selection kills unfused cells, leaving hybridomas
Screen and clone to obtain a single antibody-producing line
questions.explanation: Hybridomas provide a continuous source of one antibody; the suffix records how much sequence is human.

questions.stem: Describe how anti-TNF therapy treats inflammatory disease and explain why infection screening is needed before it is started.
markingGuide: TNF is a pro-inflammatory cytokine acting via NF-κB, causing IL-1/IL-6 and leucocyte recruitment
Anti-TNF mAbs (infliximab, adalimumab) bind TNF and neutralise it
TNF needed for granuloma maintenance, so TB can reactivate
Screen for latent TB (IGRA/TST, CXR), hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc), often HCV/HIV
Avoid live vaccines; review vaccination status
questions.explanation: The same cytokine that drives disease also protects against intracellular infection, so risk is assessed before treatment.

questions.stem: Why does anti-TNF therapy benefit patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and why can it cause serious infections?
markingGuide: TNF drives synovial inflammation and joint damage
Blocking it reduces cytokine cascade and leucocyte recruitment
TNF is required for host defence against intracellular organisms and granuloma formation
Risk of TB reactivation and other serious infections
questions.explanation: The therapeutic effect and the risk come from the same mechanism: reduced TNF signalling.
